core_claim.quote: The experience of seeing occurs when the organism masters what we call the governing laws of sensorimotor contingency.

source.citation: O'Regan JK, Noë A. A sensorimotor account of vision and visual consciousness. Behavioral and Brain Sciences 24(5):939-973 (target article), with open peer commentary and the authors' response, 973-1031, 2001

prediction.statement: If a colour patch is made to look red whenever a person looks straight at it and green whenever they look away (controlled by an eye tracker), then after training the person will come to see the central red and the peripheral green as the same colour.

first_stated.passage: The rather counterintuitive prediction from this is that after training in this situation, the observer should come to have the impression that green patches in peripheral vision and red patches in central vision are the same color.

source.citation: O'Regan JK, Noë A. A sensorimotor account of vision and visual consciousness. Behavioral and Brain Sciences 24(5):939-973 (target article), with open peer commentary and the authors' response, 973-1031, 2001

prediction.test_for: After training in which a patch's colour changes with where the eyes point, people's colour judgements shift so that the colour shown in central vision and the different colour shown in the periphery are reported as more alike (or matched as the same) than before training, compared with an untrained or non-contingent control.
prediction.test_against: After training long enough to produce adaptation on other measures, people's judgements of the central and peripheral colours are unchanged compared with a control that saw the same colours without the link to eye position.

other_statements_of_the_prediction.passage: The “armchair” experiment with colour we mentioned in section 5.8 of the target article is another counterintuitive prediction which we are currently testing, and which has met with some success (O’Regan et al. 2001).
